generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, the first stage of writing is reading the task closely. A brief such as 'Evaluate a training session plan for a youth squad' has a steer ('evaluate', which asks you to weigh, not just describe) and keywords ('training session', 'youth squad') that fix the topic. A coach reads that steer differently from how a physiologist reads 'analyse the test data', yet both must answer what was asked. A rough plan then bridges your reading and the writing itself, and a first draft turns that plan into sentences you can improve. Missing the steer is one of the most common and costly mistakes in sport assignments.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport coaching students are set the same assignment: 'Evaluate a training session plan for a youth squad.'

Tom reads the title once, spots the topic, and starts writing everything he knows about session planning. He makes no plan and pays no attention to the word 'evaluate', so the piece becomes a long description of drills that never weighs the plan's strengths against its weaknesses. The steer was missed, and a lot of effort goes into answering a question that was not asked.

Amara reads the title closely, underlines 'evaluate' and 'youth squad', and notes that the essay must weigh the session plan rather than just describe it. A quick plan sets out the plan's aims, the evidence for and against its drills, and an order. Then she writes a rough draft straight from the plan, not worrying yet about style, ready to improve it next.

Both students knew session planning. Only Amara read the task, planned, and turned that plan into a draft, the moves that make the writing answer the question.
generatedProse.summary: Writing in the School of Sport starts with understanding the task: its steer, which tells you how to answer, and its keywords, which fix what to answer. A rough plan then bridges your reading and your writing, and a first draft turns that plan into sentences you can improve. You can now read a sport brief for its steer and keywords, turn a plan into a draft, and make a sensible first move at the blank page. The next lesson is about improving that draft.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Amara do to turn her understanding into a draft?

items.text: She made a rough plan from the task and wrote a first draft straight from that plan.
She wrote down everything she knew about session planning without a plan.
She polished her opening paragraph until it was perfect before continuing.
She waited until she fully understood coaching before writing anything.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara planned from the task and drafted straight from the plan.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the plan-then-draft move, rather than a plan-free dump or endless polishing.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara made a rough plan and wrote a draft from it. Writing without a plan, perfecting one paragraph, or waiting indefinitely are not it.
